report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a range of developmental differences following the exposure of alcohol in utero.
Although not a stand-alone diagnostic criterion for FASD, sensory processing deficits are commonly observed in individuals with FASD.
The purpose of this scoping review was to review the existing evidence regarding the sensory processing differences in individuals with FASD compared to neurotypical individuals.
A scoping review of the literature was conducted investigating studies of human participants with FASD and neurotypical participants.
Studies were included if they reported on sensory processing differences between FASD and neurotypical participants.
Any measures of sensory processing and in-utero exposure to alcohol were included.
APA Psycinfo, Embase, Medline, Scopus, and CINAHL were searched for relevant studies.
A total of 1192 studies were screened for inclusion, of which 42 were extracted.
Studies investigated sensory processing differences in unisensory visual, auditory, olfactory, and somatosensory processing, multisensory integration, and sensorimotor processing.
Measures of sensory processing included imaging measures (fMRI, MRI), clinical interviews, questionnaires, behavioural tasks, psychometric tests, and electrophysiological measures (EEG, MEG, DTI).

Results indicate that differences in sensory processing exist in individuals with FASD when compared to neurotypical controls; however, these differences may vary depending on the age of participants, the type of sensory processing being measured, and other individual participant factors.

Sensory processing is defined as brain processes involved in detecting and integrating sensory inputs from the environment and generating an appropriate response (Al Qutub et al., 2024; Harrison & Hare, 2004).

text.text: Typical sensitive periods for normal sensory processing development occur from prenatal periods to early childhood (Azañón et al., 2018; Maurer & Lewis, 2013).

text.text: Taken together, previous literature on neurodevelopmental disorders suggests that impaired early sensory development impacts sensory processing in individuals with ASD, ADHD, learning disorders, and childhood-onset fluency disorders.
These impacts in sensory processing are related to deficits in higher-order cognitive functioning in individuals with these disorders.

text.text: Diagnosis of FASD is typically based on a specific pattern of birth defects following prenatal alcohol exposure including prenatal and/or postnatal growth retardation, facial dysmorphology, neurobehavioural disabilities, and central nervous system dysfunction (Denny et al., 2017), though different diagnostic codes have been developed over time (Astley & Clarren, 2000; Chudley et al., 2005; Stratton et al., 1996; more details provided in S1) The timing and amount of alcohol exposure contribute to variation in the symptoms seen in individuals with FASD.

text.text: Prenatal alcohol exposure has drastic impacts on early sensitive periods.

Research from animal models of FASD indicates that prenatal alcohol exposure can disrupt cell migration and neural plate formation, resulting in structural brain malformations including in areas responsible for sensory processing (Alsakran & Kudoh, 2021; Clark B.J. et al., 2025).

text.text: Therefore, just as with other neurodevelopmental disorders, individuals with FASD experience disruptions in the development of early sensory areas, that may impact their sensory processing.
Individuals with FASD also demonstrate impaired fine motor skills, neurosensory hearing loss, poor tandem gait, and poor hand-eye coordination (Chudley et al., 2005).

text.text: Based on this, it is reasonable to believe that just as in other neurodevelopmental disorders, atypical sensitive periods and deficits in higher-order processes in FASD may be related to deficits in sensory processing.

The purpose of this review, the first of its kind, is to investigate the state of the literature and provide an overview of which areas of sensory processing are impacted by FASD, and how that compares to neurotypical individuals.
This scoping review follows the methodology described by the JBI Guidance for Scoping Reviews (Peters et al., 2020) and the PRISMA guidelines for scoping reviews (Tricco et al., 2018).

text.text: Included studies were original, peer-reviewed research works that investigated sensory processing in human participants of any age with FASD (including fetal alcohol syndrome, partial fetal alcohol syndrome, alcohol related neurodevelopmental disorder, and prenatal exposure to alcohol/ethanol) compared to neurotypical participants (healthy controls with no reported neurodevelopmental disorders).
Sensory processing was purposefully kept broad to provide a general overview of sensory processing differences in FASD.
Any study investigating the perception of a stimulus (uinsensory or multisensory processing, sensory sensitivity or reactivity, sensory gating, and/or sensorimotor skills) was included.
Any measure of sensory processing was included, including behavioural, neural, questionnaire, and qualitative studies.
Studies were excluded if they investigated differences in sensory organs without assessing the response to a sensory stimulus.
Case studies, dissertations, reviews, conference abstracts, books, and book chapters were excluded.
Studies were also excluded if they did not specify whether the control group was made up of neurotypical/typically developing individuals.
The searches were conducted across five databases on October 23, 2025: APA Psycinfo, Embase, Medline, Scopus and CINAHL.
A sample search strategy can be found in Table 1, with all search studies attached in S1.

text.text: Search results were imported to Covidence (Veritas Health Innovation, 2025) to be independently screened.

Appropriate subject headings for each database (not applicable for SCOPUS) and all keywords synonymous with "sensory processing", "sensory perception", "fetal alcohol spectrum disorder", "prenatal exposure to alcohol", and "prenatal exposure to ethanol" were included in the searches.
A total of 2085 studies were identified in the database search and uploaded to Covidence by X.X. 876 duplicates were identified by Covidence and another 17 duplicates were identified manually.
This left 1192 studies for screening.
Titles and abstracts were independently reviewed by X.X. and X.X. or X.X. for inclusion eligibility using Covidence.

Discrepancies between the three reviewers were discussed and a decision was made based on whether each study investigated some aspect of sensory processing and had a typically developing control group.
Studies where this was not clear from the abstract were included in the full-text review.

Following the title and abstract review, 128 studies were included for full text review, which was completed by X.X., and X.X. or X.X. Following the full text review, 86 studies were excluded because they were not peer reviewed articles, did not include a typically-developing control group, or did not measure or compare sensory processing between groups.
The final analysis included 42 studies.

The Sensory Profile is a commonly used measure of sensory processing behaviours in daily experiences (C. Brown & Dunn, 2002; Dunn, 2014).

text.text: These behaviours are grouped into four quadrants: low registration (length/intensity of stimuli needed to respond), sensation seeking (level of interest and pleasure associated with sensory stimuli), sensory sensitivity (ability to notice sensory stimuli), and sensation avoiding (need to control amount/intensity of sensory stimuli).

In preschool aged children with confirmed low-moderate prenatal alcohol exposure, no differences on any of the Infant/Toddler Sensory Profile quadrants exist when compared to neurotypical children (Bakhireva et al., 2018).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that general sensory processing differences seem more pronounced in children with more severe prenatal alcohol exposure compared to children with low-moderate prenatal exposure of alcohol.
Research suggests differences in sensory neural pathways between individuals with FASD and neurotypical individuals.

During resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), children with FASD demonstrate reductions in connectivity between the medial prefrontal cortex and anterior supramarginal gyrus when compared to neurotypical children, suggesting potential disruptions in sensory-motor integration (Alsameen et al., 2025).

text.text: Further differences were also found in the frontal parietal network, with altered connectivity between the posterior temporal fusiform cortex, temporal occipital fusiform cortex, and parahippocampal cortex, suggesting dysregulation in networks associated with visuomotor control.

Findings using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) also suggest lower white matter integrity in the right lateral temporal lobe and bilateral splenium in adolescents and young adults with FASD compared to neurotypical controls, suggesting white matter deficits in brain areas associated with auditory, visual, and somatosensory processing in FASD (Pinner et al., 2020; Sowell et al., 2008).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that individuals with FASD have dysregulated networks associated with sensory processing, specifically, motor and sensory integration networks, and white matter tracts associated with auditory, somatosensory, and visual processing.
The most commonly investigated topic in this review was visual sensory processing (investigated in 26 studies).
Adolescents and children with FASD were reported to demonstrate pronounced differences in visual processing compared to neurotypical adolescents and children.

Alcohol-exposed adolescents and children demonstrate lower accuracy rates of detecting basic visual stimuli (such as shapes or letters) compared to neurotypical adolescents and children, suggesting impaired responsivity (Coles et al., 2002; Mattson et al., 2006; Paolozza A. et al., 2013 Paolozza A. et al., , 2014 Paolozza A. et al., , 2014;; Paolozza et al., 2015) and contrast sensitivity (Vernescu et al., 2012) to visual stimuli.

In magnetoencephalography (MEG) studies of visual processing, adolescents and young adults with FASD demonstrate delayed M100 amplitude and latency compared to neurotypical controls (Coffman et al., 2013; Pervin et al., 2022).

text.text: The M100 component indicates early cortical processing of sensory input.
Delayed M100 amplitude and latency in response to visual stimuli in these studies suggests less accurate and efficient processing of visual stimuli.
These delays seem to be more pronounced in peripheral vision in individuals with FASD when compared to healthy controls.

M100 latency is also delayed in adolescents with FASD compared to neurotypical adolescents according to MEG measures during saccadic eye movement tasks, suggesting delayed early visual responses in FASD compared to neurotypical adolescents (Stephen et al., 2013).

DTI results indicate that children with prenatal alcohol exposure have lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean diffusivity in multiple white matter tracts related to visual processing compared to neurotypical children on eye movement tasks (Paolozza et al., 2017).

text.text: This finding suggests slower and less efficient transmission of visual information between visual processing areas.

Interestingly, some studies do not report differences in reaction time or accuracy between children with FASD and neurotypical children in response to visual stimuli (Paolozza et al., 2016; Stephen et al., 2013).

Auditory processing has also been commonly investigated in people with FASD, suggesting differences in auditory perception when compared to neurotypical people.

text.formatted: Children and adolescents with FASD demonstrate slower reaction times in response to auditory stimuli when compared to neurotypical children, suggesting deficits in sound perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Coles et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Some studies suggest that while their reaction times to auditory stimuli do not differ from neurotypical children, children with FASD are less accurate at detecting auditory stimuli (Mattson et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Some studies suggest that while their reaction times to auditory stimuli do not differ from neurotypical children, children with FASD are less accurate at detecting auditory stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Mattson et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Children and adolescents with FASD also demonstrate differences in the electrophysiological processing of auditory information in cortical pathways according to electrophysiological (EEG) measures., Children with FASD show differences in N1, N2, and P50 amplitudes compared to neurotypical children during auditory oddball paradigms.
Delayed amplitudes in these components suggest weaker early filtering, encoding, and processing of early sensory input.
Therefore, these findings suggest that early stages of auditory processing may be impacted by fetal alcohol exposure (Kabella et al., 2018; Stephen et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Therefore, these findings suggest that early stages of auditory processing may be impacted by fetal alcohol exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Kabella et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Stephen et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence from MEG recordings during auditory stimuli presentation are somewhat mixed.

Some studies indicate small, delayed latencies in M100 and M200 in children with FASD compared to neurotypical children (Stephen et al., 2012), while other studies suggest no group differences (Coffman et al., 2020; Kabella et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Some studies indicate small, delayed latencies in M100 and M200 in children with FASD compared to neurotypical children <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Stephen et al., 2012)</ref>, while other studies suggest no group differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Coffman et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Kabella et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Adolescents with FASD do however demonstrate decreased gamma oscillatory power in response to auditory stimuli compared to neurotypical controls (Bolaños et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Adolescents with FASD do however demonstrate decreased gamma oscillatory power in response to auditory stimuli compared to neurotypical controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Bolaños et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Decreased gamma oscillatory power is indicative of less neural synchrony in response to stimuli, suggesting impairments in the early sensory processing of auditory stimuli.

In neurophysiological paradigms, children with FASD demonstrate deficits in auditory processing when compared to typically developing controls; however, these differences were not statistically significant (Kable et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In neurophysiological paradigms, children with FASD demonstrate deficits in auditory processing when compared to typically developing controls; however, these differences were not statistically significant <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Kable et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers note that deficits in visual processing were significant in the FASD group and suggest therefore that the visual modality may be more vulnerable to the impact of prenatal alcohol exposure than the auditory modality is.

Additional research using such paradigms is needed to better compare the auditory processing differences between individuals with FASD and typically developing controls, and whether these differences extend across other modalities.
Adults with FASD display deficits in auditory attention when compared to neurotypical controls.

They have been found to perform significantly lower on psychometric tests of auditory attention when compared to neurotypical control, and these deficits in auditory perception are stronger than deficits in visual perception (Connor et al., 1999).
text.formatted: They have been found to perform significantly lower on psychometric tests of auditory attention when compared to neurotypical control, and these deficits in auditory perception are stronger than deficits in visual perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Connor et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, MEG studies report shorter latencies of P50 and N1 components over auditory cortex in adolescents and young adults with FASD compared to neurotypicals (Tesche et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Interestingly, MEG studies report shorter latencies of P50 and N1 components over auditory cortex in adolescents and young adults with FASD compared to neurotypicals <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">(Tesche et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Shorter latencies of the P50 component suggest a slower ability to filter out irrelevant stimuli while shorter latencies of the N1 component suggest a decrease in the efficiency of early attention.
Adolescents and young adults with FASD therefore demonstrate decreased rates of filtering out irrelevant auditory information and efficiently attending to relevant auditory information.

Taken together, these findings suggest that while behavioural and neurophysiological deficits in auditory processing may persist in adulthood, additional research is needed with adult populations to confirm these findings.
Adolescents with prenatal alcohol exposure do not demonstrate differences in speech perception compared to unexposed adolescents (Simões et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Adolescents with prenatal alcohol exposure do not demonstrate differences in speech perception compared to unexposed adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">(Simões et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, children with FASD demonstrate difficulties in perceiving and repeating words during dichotic listening tasks when compared to neurotypical controls.

Dichotic listening paradigms assess hemispheric asymmetry for speech and language processing and presume that dichotic listening asymmetry relies on the functional status of the corpus callosum (Westerhausen & Kompus, 2018).
text.formatted: Dichotic listening paradigms assess hemispheric asymmetry for speech and language processing and presume that dichotic listening asymmetry relies on the functional status of the corpus callosum <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">(Westerhausen & Kompus, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Using this paradigm, typically developing participants with left-hemispheric dominance report the stimuli presented in their right-ear with higher probability than their left ear.
In children with FASD, however, this pattern of perception to the auditory processing of words was not seen, suggesting reduced auditory lateralization in children with FASD (Domellöf et al., 2009).
text.formatted: In children with FASD, however, this pattern of perception to the auditory processing of words was not seen, suggesting reduced auditory lateralization in children with FASD <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Domellöf et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Further, children with FASD also seem to perform worse on psychometric tasks of auditory word and non-word discrimination, suggesting potential deficits in auditory speech processing in FASD (Terband et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Further, children with FASD also seem to perform worse on psychometric tasks of auditory word and non-word discrimination, suggesting potential deficits in auditory speech processing in FASD <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Terband et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that complex auditory perception may only be impacted in young age, though further research is needed to support these findings.
Only one study investigated olfactory processing differences in people with FASD compared to neurotypical people.
Using an odor identification task, children and adolescents with prenatal alcohol exposure were significantly worse at identifying odors when compared to neurotypical controls (Bower et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Using an odor identification task, children and adolescents with prenatal alcohol exposure were significantly worse at identifying odors when compared to neurotypical controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Bower et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Further study of differences in olfactory perception between people with FASD and neurotypical controls is needed to better understand these findings.

MEG recordings during somatosensory stimulus presentation indicate decreased gamma oscillatory power in adolescents with FASD compared to neurotypical controls, suggesting impairments in the efficiency of processing somatosensory stimuli (Bolaños et al., 2017).
text.formatted: MEG recordings during somatosensory stimulus presentation indicate decreased gamma oscillatory power in adolescents with FASD compared to neurotypical controls, suggesting impairments in the efficiency of processing somatosensory stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Bolaños et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Further, FASD adolescents and young adults demonstrate delayed M200 response latency to somatosensory stimuli when compared to neurotypical controls (Coffman et al., 2020); however, somatosensory M100 response latency do not differ between groups.
text.formatted: Further, FASD adolescents and young adults demonstrate delayed M200 response latency to somatosensory stimuli when compared to neurotypical controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Coffman et al., 2020)</ref>; however, somatosensory M100 response latency do not differ between groups.

text.text: These findings seem to suggest intact early somatosensory encoding, with potentially delayed higher-level cognitive processing.

Interestingly FASD adolescents and young adults do demonstrate reduced amplitude of M100 and M200 responses; however, these seem to be limited to the left hemisphere only and may therefore not be indicative of overall peripheral deficits in FASD (Coffman et al., 2020)..
text.formatted: Interestingly FASD adolescents and young adults do demonstrate reduced amplitude of M100 and M200 responses; however, these seem to be limited to the left hemisphere only and may therefore not be indicative of overall peripheral deficits in FASD <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Coffman et al., 2020)</ref>..

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest potential deficits in processing somatosensory information in individuals with FASD.
Future research is needed in this area to replicate these findings.
In addition to differences in unisensory perception, differences in the perception of multisensory stimuli have also been investigated between individuals with FASD and neurotypicals.
MEG studies have identified reduced gamma power in response to audio-tactile stimuli in FASD adolescents compared to neurotypical adolescents (Bolaños et al., 2017).
text.formatted: MEG studies have identified reduced gamma power in response to audio-tactile stimuli in FASD adolescents compared to neurotypical adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Bolaños et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest impaired integration of audio-tactile stimuli, suggesting restricted abilities to process multisensory stimuli in daily life in adolescents with FASD.

Interestingly, some research has found no significant differences in M100 response latency to audio-tactile stimuli when compared to neurotypical controls, suggesting no differences in multisensory integration between the two groups according to MEG results (Coffman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Interestingly, some research has found no significant differences in M100 response latency to audio-tactile stimuli when compared to neurotypical controls, suggesting no differences in multisensory integration between the two groups according to MEG results <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Coffman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, the paradigms used in these studies do not account for sensitivity differences in participants.

Considering participants' unisensory detection thresholds is important when assessing multisensory integration as it ensures that all stimuli are presented at perception matched levels for each participant, thus controlling for participants' unisensory accuracy of detecting the sensory stimuli used in studies.

Thus, future research should investigate multisensory integration responses after first controlling for participants' sensitivity levels, to ensure any gains in multisensory integration are in fact as a result of the multiple stimuli presented.

Individuals with FASD may also demonstrate differences in sensorimotor development, processing, and behaviour., Children and adolescents with FASD and prenatal alcohol exposure perform significantly lower than neurotypical children and adolescents on clinical and behavioural measures of sensorimotor outcomes, including on measures of visual-motor development, gait, balance, motor proficiency, and overall static and dynamic movement (T. Jirikowic et al., 2008; T. L. Jirikowic et al., 2013; Korkman et al., 1994; Lidstone, Miah, Poston, Beasley, & Dufek, 2020a; Williams et al., 2014).

text.text: Visual-motor integration has been frequently examined in individuals with FASD, specifically with regards to their scores on the Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration (Beery & Beery, 2016).
text.formatted: Visual-motor integration has been frequently examined in individuals with FASD, specifically with regards to their scores on the Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Beery & Beery, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence is inconsistent on whether FASD is associated with differences in visual-motor integration relative to typically developing participants.

Significant group differences in visual-motor integration scores have been found in children with FASD when compared with neurotypical controls (Janzen, 1995; Sowell et al., 2008), though children and adolescents with FASD do not differ from neurotypical children in their motor response to dynamic and static visual stimuli (Lidstone, Miah, Poston, Beasley, & Dufek, 2020b; Lidstone, Miah, Poston, Beasley, Mostofsky, et al., 2020), in their response times to visual-motor stimuli (Simmons et al., 2006), or their use of visual feedback in drawing tasks (Simmons et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Significant group differences in visual-motor integration scores have been found in children with FASD when compared with neurotypical controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Janzen, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Sowell et al., 2008)</ref>, though children and adolescents with FASD do not differ from neurotypical children in their motor response to dynamic and static visual stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Lidstone, Miah, Poston, Beasley, & Dufek, 2020b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Lidstone, Miah, Poston, Beasley, Mostofsky, et al., 2020)</ref>, in their response times to visual-motor stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Simmons et al., 2006)</ref>, or their use of visual feedback in drawing tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">(Simmons et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest behavioural impairments in visual-motor integration may not be as apparent in children with FASD when compared to neurotypical controls.
While not considered a core diagnostic criterion, sensory processing differences have been reported in people with FASD.
Thus, this review sought to determine what sensory processing differences exist between people with FASD and neurotypical controls.
This review of 60 papers documents reported differences in unisensory perception of visual, auditory, olfactory, and somatosensory stimuli, multisensory integration, and sensorimotor processing.
Studies investigated these differences using various measures, ranging from questionnaire to neuroimaging studies.
Certain areas of sensory processing in FASD seem to have more pronounced deficits when compared to neurotypical individuals.

Specifically, children and adolescents with FASD demonstrated deficits in somatosensory processing (Bolaños et al., 2017; Coffman et al., 2020), olfactory perception (Bower et al., 2013), It is important to note, however, that fewer studies investigated these areas of sensory processing than areas of sensory processing that demonstrated greater variability in results.
text.formatted: Specifically, children and adolescents with FASD demonstrated deficits in somatosensory processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Bolaños et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Coffman et al., 2020)</ref>, olfactory perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Bower et al., 2013)</ref>, It is important to note, however, that fewer studies investigated these areas of sensory processing than areas of sensory processing that demonstrated greater variability in results.

text.text: Thus, future research in the processing of somatosensory, and olfactory stimuli and motion is needed to understand whether these findings replicate.
People with FASD show greater variability in sensory processing of other sensory stimuli, including static visual, auditory, sensorimotor, and multisensory stimuli.
Findings suggest that the degree to which people with FASD differ in their processing of these stimuli varies depending on the age of participants and the measures used to assess the processing.
Levels of prenatal alcohol exposure and other participant factors may also contribute to the reported differences in sensory processing.
Results in sensory processing may vary depending on the age of participants.
Specifically, children and adolescents seemed to demonstrate differences in various areas of sensory processing; however, fewer studies investigated differences in sensory processing in adults.

While young adults with FASD seem to have results consistent with children and adolescents (Coffman et al., 2020; Pinner et al., 2020; Sowell et al., 2008; Tesche et al., 2015), differences in sensory processing in older adults are less clear (Connor et al., 1999).
text.formatted: While young adults with FASD seem to have results consistent with children and adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Coffman et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Pinner et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Sowell et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Tesche et al., 2015)</ref>, differences in sensory processing in older adults are less clear <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Connor et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, age may play a crucial role in sensory processing differences in people with FASD, with potential evidence suggesting impairments in early sensory processing may be compensated for overtime.

This would be consistent with research in other neurodevelopmental disorders, which suggests that with time, people with neurodevelopmental disorders may catch-up to typically developing peers, resulting in fewer differences seen between groups (Foxe et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This would be consistent with research in other neurodevelopmental disorders, which suggests that with time, people with neurodevelopmental disorders may catch-up to typically developing peers, resulting in fewer differences seen between groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Foxe et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, additional research is needed to confirm these findings, perhaps employing longitudinal study designs to examine long-term effects of FASD on sensory processing.
Various measures were used to assess sensory processing differences in FASD, and results varied depending on the measures used.

For example, despite a lack of differences in task accuracy and reaction time, children and adolescents with FASD still demonstrate differences in neural pathways that support sensory perception when compared to neurotypical children (Stephen et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, despite a lack of differences in task accuracy and reaction time, children and adolescents with FASD still demonstrate differences in neural pathways that support sensory perception when compared to neurotypical children <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">(Stephen et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are consistent with studies of behavioural and neural sensory differences in other neurodevelopmental disorders, where studies report differences in sensory processing based on neurophysiological and electrophysiological findings despite behavioural accuracy and reaction times remaining unaffected (Choi et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2025; Hames et al., 2016; Pierce et al., 2021).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with studies of behavioural and neural sensory differences in other neurodevelopmental disorders, where studies report differences in sensory processing based on neurophysiological and electrophysiological findings despite behavioural accuracy and reaction times remaining unaffected <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Choi et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Ghosh et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Hames et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Pierce et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These results suggest that individuals with FASD may demonstrate altered neural pathways and responses, but that these differences may not always translate to behavioural differences when compared to neurotypical individuals.
However, even using similar measures, heterogeneity is seen in sensory processing in those with FASD.

For example, greater variability in Sensory Profile scores is reported in people with FASD when compared to neurotypical controls, whereas scores on the Sensory Processing Measure suggest deficits in sensory processing in people with FASD when compared to controls.
Similarly, findings from behavioural studies are mixed depending on the paradigm used and whether low-or high-level sensory processing is being assessed.
Finally, variations in results were found when using different types of electrophysiological techniques (EEG vs.
MEG vs.
cardiac orienting responses).

These findings are consistent with studies of sensory processing in other neurodevelopmental disorders, which have suggested that different measures may capture different areas of sensory processing, thus potentially resulting in differing findings across studies (DuBois et al., 2017; Schulz & Stevenson, 2020 , 2022).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with studies of sensory processing in other neurodevelopmental disorders, which have suggested that different measures may capture different areas of sensory processing, thus potentially resulting in differing findings across studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(DuBois et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">Schulz & Stevenson, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: It is the case that different areas of sensory processing were studied in the following review, which may contribute to the different findings reported.
Further, these differences may also speak to the vast heterogeneity of FASD symptoms, which may be captured differently based on the measures used.
Future research may seek to investigate how FASD impacts specific areas of sensory processing, to better understand the impact of prenatal alcohol exposure on these areas.
Results suggested that the level of prenatal alcohol exposure may contribute to differences in sensory processing.

Some studies reported no differences between individuals with low-to-moderate levels of prenatal alcohol exposure when compared to neurotypical individuals (Bakhireva et al., 2018; Kable et al., 2021), suggesting that low levels of prenatal alcohol exposure may not result in impairments in sensory processing.
text.formatted: Some studies reported no differences between individuals with low-to-moderate levels of prenatal alcohol exposure when compared to neurotypical individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Bakhireva et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Kable et al., 2021)</ref>, suggesting that low levels of prenatal alcohol exposure may not result in impairments in sensory processing.

text.text: Further, the amount and timing of prenatal alcohol exposure may impact sensory processing.

Results indicated that binge drinking in early pregnancy with continued drinking at low levels throughout pregnancy is associated with sensory processing deficits compared to no prenatal exposure (Halliday et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Results indicated that binge drinking in early pregnancy with continued drinking at low levels throughout pregnancy is associated with sensory processing deficits compared to no prenatal exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Halliday et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, not all studies reported the amount and timing of the prenatal alcohol exposure.
It is important to consider differences in the level of prenatal alcohol exposure given that some areas of sensory processing are more sensitive to the developmental impacts of alcohol exposure.

As a result, areas such as olfaction and audition are impacted by very low levels of alcohol exposure due to use of and reliance on delicate cell receptors, likely contributing to distinct group differences in these areas (Imamura, 2024; Römer et al., 2020).

text.text: Further, research suggests that greater amounts of prenatal alcohol exposure is associated with greater impairments in sensory processing, with some studiese suggesting these impacts are only present in the visual and auditory domain, but others suggesting these are more widespread processing differences (Flak et al., 2014; T. L. Jirikowic et al., 2020).

text.text: Variability in FASD symptoms is also impacted by factors such as maternal and fetal genetics (Dodge et al., 2014; Fish et al., 2017), timing of exposure (Sulik, 2014), dosage and patterning of exposure (Bandoli et al., 2019; Feldman et al., 2019), and nutritional factors (Keen et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Variability in FASD symptoms is also impacted by factors such as maternal and fetal genetics <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Dodge et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Fish et al., 2017)</ref>, timing of exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Sulik, 2014)</ref>, dosage and patterning of exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Bandoli et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Feldman et al., 2019)</ref>, and nutritional factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Keen et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Any of these factors may contribute to differences in fetal development that can impact sensory processing.

Future research may seek to understand how these factors impact sensory processing differences between those with FASD and neurotypical controls, and how sensory processing differs within those diagnosed with FASD based on these factors.
Not all studies provided information regarding the co-occurring diagnoses that participants had.

Thus, while all individuals included in this review had FASD/prenatal alcohol exposure, some may have also had other co-occurring disorders that may have been contributing to their sensory processing deficits.

For example, FASD commonly co-occurs with other neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD (28.4%) and other intellectual and developmental disorders (19.4%) (Attell et al., 2025), which may be contributing to sensory processing differences on their own.
text.formatted: For example, FASD commonly co-occurs with other neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD (28.4%) and other intellectual and developmental disorders (19.4%) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Attell et al., 2025)</ref>, which may be contributing to sensory processing differences on their own.

text.text: Thus, in studies that did not specify whether children also had co-occurring disorders, it is hard to attribute the sensory processing differences found to FASD alone.
Additionally, not all studies reported on whether mothers who had drunk alcohol during pregnancy also used additional substances.

Some research has linked prenatal cocaine and marijuana usage to deficits in sensory and information processing (Bailey & Osborne, 2023; Chiriboga et al., 2009), which may also be attributing to differences in sensory processing reported in the studies in this review.

text.text: Future research may be needed to investigate sensory processing differences that are unique to children with FASD.

However, it is important to note that this may not be representative of the general FASD population, given the high prevalence rates of co-occurring psychopathologies in this population (Attell et al., 2025).

text.text: There are a number of limitations to consider in the following study.

The broadness of the review was purposeful to allow for large inclusion of sensory processing differences in FASD, however, made it difficult to draw conclusions on overarching differences in sensory processing in FASD given the vast differences in measures used to assess sensory processing.

Further, given only studies with a neurotypical/typically developing control group were included, some studies of sensory processing in FASD were excluded which did not include a clear neurotypical or typically developing control group, as they did not allow for comparisons between groups.
Thus, there may be additional research findings that may clarify some of the discrepancies between results reviewed in the present study that were not included in this review.
The following review investigated the sensory processing differences between people with FASD and those with typical development.

Findings from 42, peer-reviewed studies indicate that FASD seems to be associated with differences in the unisensory perception of visual, auditory, olfactory, and somatosensory stimuli, multisensory processing, and sensorimotor processing when compared to typical development.

It is important to note the vast heterogeneity in results across studies, which may be due to differences in ages of participants, measures of sensory processing used, level of prenatal alcohol exposure, and other individual participant factors.

Future research should continue to investigate sensory processing differences in those with FASD, to confirm whether differences are consistent across individuals with FASD when compared to those with typical development, while taking into account participant comorbidities and other factors contributing to heterogeneity in FASD symptoms.
